title: Dave Gustafson & Co. v. State
summary: A graduated daily charge for delay in completing a public highway was enforceable as a reasonable advance estimate of losses that were difficult to measure.
notes:
The notes ask whether an independently delayed bridge would change the result and compare legitimate alternative performances with penalty labels. The hypothetical bridge was not a fact of Gustafson itself.

83 S.D. 160, 156 N.W.2d 185, decided February 13, 1968. The October 1963 contract recited that time was essential because of the costs and public inconvenience of delay, and the graduated schedule set $210 per day for contracts between $500,001 and $1,000,000.

sections.Parties: Dave Gustafson & Company was the highway-surfacing contractor. The State of South Dakota was the owner that withheld stipulated delay damages from the payment otherwise due.
sections.Material Facts: Gustafson surfaced a new highway running parallel to an older road, which remained open during and after construction. The project finished sixty-seven days late. The contract contained a graduated daily-damages schedule tied to the size of the contract. For projects over $500,000 and not over $1 million, the rate was $210 a day. The state accordingly withheld $14,070 from the $530,724.14 otherwise due for the work. The continuing availability of the old road furnished a reason to question whether the state had actually suffered loss equal to the specified charge.
sections.Procedural History: The contractor sued for the withheld payment. The trial court upheld the state’s reliance on the clause. The South Dakota Supreme Court affirmed in 1968.
sections.Issue: Was the stipulated daily charge an enforceable estimate of delay loss or an unenforceable penalty?
sections.Holding: The clause was enforceable as liquidated damages. The court found difficult-to-measure injury, a reasonable effort to estimate compensation, and a reasonable relationship between the graduated rate and probable loss.
sections.Reasoning:
Highway delay can cause public inconvenience, deprivation of use, and additional costs that are extremely difficult to price accurately. The absence of a simple market measure gives the parties a legitimate reason to agree on a formula in advance. The schedule also varied with the size of the project and multiplied the rate by days of delay. The court regarded those features as evidence of an attempt to track the scale and duration of injury, rather than impose an arbitrary punishment.

The court assessed the stipulated amount against probable damage at the time of contracting and did not require the state to prove a precisely equal post-breach loss. The older road’s availability did not eliminate all of the new project’s delayed benefits. The decision therefore provides a contrast to formulas that ignore expenses saved or impose the same payment for substantially different breaches.

textbookImport.basis: Study paraphrase of the supplied tenth-edition casebook. No current-law/citator review.

learning.why: This decision supplies a successful example of advance damages estimation. Compare its size-and-duration formula with the saved-cost problem in Lake River and the gross-receipts problem in Wasserman’s.

topics.remedies: Enforces a reasonable agreed measure for a difficult-to-value public loss.
topics.liquidated-damages: Connects the formula’s graduated structure to anticipated injury.
topics.certainty: Explains why difficulty measuring loss can support a stipulated remedy.
topics.stipulated-remedies: The case applies the liquidated-damages-versus-penalty test to a graduated per-day delay charge.
topics.certainty-damages: The clause was upheld because the public's loss from highway delay was inherently difficult to prove with certainty.
